No reachable source names the city, the state, or the hospital; the record of his life opens with a date and no place. Twenty-five years later he will hold a computer science degree from the University of Washington, and that campus is the first ground any document actually puts under his feet. He will spend his working life arguing that written records are the weak point of every property system. The first record of him is missing the place.

stops.campa: David Chaum's company sits in Amsterdam, building Ecash out of the blind signature Chaum invented, a scheme that lets a bank certify a coin it cannot afterwards recognize. Szabo works there on the project during the 1990s. It is the closest anyone has come to digital cash that spends like paper. The bank still exists, still issues, and still has to be trusted not to inflate or refuse. That flaw sits in the shape of the design rather than in its mathematics, and nothing added inside the scheme removes it.

stops.name: Amsterdam, the blind signature
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The mechanics of Chaum's blind signature are attested in the cryptographic literature; the date here is a placement default inside the DigiCash years, and no source places Szabo in a particular room or year. The RSA lineage is attested through rivest_shamir_adleman.journey.json, whose 545 Technology Square pin carries the February 1978 publication.
stops.campa: The blind signature works like a carbon-lined envelope: the customer seals a serial number the bank never sees, the bank signs through the paper, and the coin comes out valid and untraceable. It is built on the function Ronald Rivest, Adi Shamir, and Leonard Adleman published from 545 Technology Square in 1978. Chaum has solved the customer's privacy and left issuance alone. Most of the building reads that as the finished job. Szabo locates the remaining hole in the bank itself, which must still be trusted about how many coins exist.

stops.name: Amsterdam, a computerized transaction protocol
stops.date_confidence: Essay and 1994 date attested: Wikipedia, 'Nick Szabo', and the Nakamoto Institute library, which reprints 'Smart Contracts' (1994) at nakamotoinstitute.org/library/smart-contracts/. Place NOT attested and actively uncertain: the gathering pass placed him in Seattle in 1994 and the verification pass rejected that, since the only documented 1990s location is DigiCash in Amsterdam. stops.campa: In 1994 he writes the essay that gives the idea its name. A smart contract, he proposes, is not a figure of speech: it is a protocol that performs the terms rather than describing them, so that enforcement lives in the machinery instead of in a court. Alongside it he sketches smart property, ownership embedded in the thing owned. The essay circulates on the networks rather than in a journal. Two decades will pass before anyone builds a system that runs what it specifies, and by then his name will be fastened to a currency he says he did not write.

stops.campa: He designs bit gold. A participant solves a computational puzzle nobody can solve cheaply, the solution is timestamped and published, and the string of bits that results is expensive by construction and cheap to check. Chain each solution to the one before and the sequence carries its own history. No bank issues it. No registry can be forged without redoing the work. He is not claiming to invent money; he says he is copying, into cyberspace, the properties that made gold difficult to counterfeit and difficult to inflate.

stops.campa: The same year he publishes 'Secure Property Titles with Owner Authority', which asks what a land registry would look like if no government held it. His answer is a replicated database kept by servers that can tolerate a fraction of themselves being dishonest, so that title survives the burning of any single archive. He argues from history rather than from cryptography: he has read what happens to property when the records office changes hands. Two decades later the same design will be sold as a blockchain asset registry.

stops.name: Unlocated, trusted third parties are security holes

stops.campa: He publishes 'Trusted Third Parties Are Security Holes', the essay that states the rule the rest of his work follows from. Every point in a protocol where a party simply has to be believed is a point that will eventually be attacked, bought, subpoenaed, or mistaken, and the cost of that hole is paid afterwards by everyone who uses the system. The argument turns on where that expense sits rather than on anyone's honesty. He had watched the question from inside Chaum's company seven years before, and had not stopped looking at it since.

stops.campa: In 'Shelling Out: The Origins of Money' he goes back behind coinage, to shell beads and wampum and the stone discs of Yap, and argues that money began as collectibles: objects costly to make, hard to fake, easy to carry, and therefore good for settling accounts between people who could neither trust each other nor remember. Money in this account is older than the state and is not the state's invention. The essay becomes the standing citation for anyone arguing that a currency needs no government in order to be a currency.

stops.name: Unenumerated, the bit gold post
stops.date_confidence: Attested, with a contradiction resolved rather than left open. The live page at unenumerated.blogspot.com/2005/12/bit-gold.html carries a timestamp of 27 December 2008, and the gathering pass reported the year as contradicted. Verification settled it for 2005: the Satoshi Nakamoto Institute dates the essay 29 December 2005, the Blogger permalink path is /2005/12/, and the Internet Archive holds a capture of that exact URL from 29 March 2006, which rules out creation in 2008. stops.campa: Seven years after designing it he writes bit gold up on Unenumerated, his blog, and posts it in the last days of December 2005. The post sets out the puzzle, the timestamp, the chain, and the problem he cannot solve: the pieces are not fungible, because a puzzle solved in one year costs a different quantity of computer time than the same puzzle solved in another. He credits Finney's RPOW. Then the post sits where he left it for three years, read by almost nobody, until an anonymous paper makes it retrospectively famous.
